headline: New Hampshire judge denies emergency bid to pause Medicaid transgender-care rule
dek: A federal judge rejected a temporary restraining order sought by four New Hampshire families, leaving the Oct. 13 coverage cutoff in place for now while a preliminary-injunction fight moves toward an Oct. 30 hearing.
body: A federal judge in New Hampshire has rejected an emergency request from four families who are challenging a federal rule that would end Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program funding for gender-dysphoria treatment for young people. The Oct. 5 order did not decide whether the rule is lawful. It denied only the families’ request for a temporary restraining order while their broader request for a preliminary injunction proceeds. The [U.S. District Court order](https://litigationtracker.law.georgetown.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Goe_2026.10.05_ORDER-ON-MOTION-FOR-PRELIMINARY-INJUNCTION.pdf) says the case is Goe et al. v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Civil No. 26-cv-803-SM-TSM.

The plaintiffs filed suit Oct. 1 under pseudonyms to protect their privacy. The [ACLU of New Hampshire](https://www.aclu-nh.org/cases/goe-et-al-v-u-s-department-of-health-and-human-services-et-al/) says the case represents four New Hampshire teenagers and their families and was brought with GLAD Law and the National Center for LGBTQ Rights. The groups are challenging a rule issued in August by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. They say it will cut off federal Medicaid and CHIP funding on Oct. 13 for medications and other treatment for gender dysphoria, including care that a patient’s doctor has determined is medically necessary.

The families asked for a preliminary injunction stopping enforcement of the rule and added that, if the court could not decide that motion before Oct. 13, it should issue an emergency temporary restraining order protecting the named plaintiffs. Judge Steven J. McAuliffe wrote that the filing did not address the specific requirements for a temporary restraining order under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65(b). In particular, the plaintiffs did not submit an affidavit clearly showing that immediate and irreparable harm would occur before the government could respond. The judge also wrote that the facts presented did not suggest the kind of emergency required for that form of relief.

That ruling leaves the case’s central legal questions open. The order does not validate the federal rule, reject the families’ arguments about Medicaid law or equal protection, or resolve what treatment any plaintiff will ultimately receive. It means only that the court will consider the preliminary-injunction request on the ordinary schedule rather than imposing an immediate, temporary shield before the government files its response. The coverage change remains scheduled to take effect Oct. 13 unless another court order or administrative action changes the timetable.

A scheduling order entered Oct. 6 sets the next milestones. The federal defendants’ response to the preliminary-injunction motion is due Oct. 15, the families’ reply is due Oct. 22, and the court has set a hearing for 10 a.m. Oct. 30. The [Georgetown University Health Care Litigation Tracker](https://litigationtracker.law.georgetown.edu/litigation/goe-et-al-v-department-of-health-and-human-services-et-al/) lists briefing as ongoing and identifies the case as a challenge to federal health-funding policy. Those dates give the litigation a defined path even though the federal funding deadline arrives before the hearing.

The dispute has a specific New Hampshire dimension. [New Hampshire Public Radio](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-02/nh-families-sue-trump-administration-medicaid-funding-transgender-services) reported that the four families are low-income households and that the teenage plaintiffs are transgender girls who use services that would no longer be covered under the change. NHPR described puberty-blocking medication and hormone therapy as examples of care affected by the Medicaid rule. Because the families are proceeding anonymously, public filings identify them through pseudonyms rather than names.

NHPR also reported that New Hampshire is the only New England state with a law banning most gender-affirming health care for transgender youth. That state law, signed by Gov. Kelly Ayotte last year, included an exception for young people already receiving care before the state restriction took effect, according to the station. The federal case presents a different question: whether federal funding rules can prevent Medicaid and CHIP from paying for care even when state policy and a patient’s doctors would otherwise allow it.

Another lawsuit brought by 22 state attorneys general is challenging the same federal Medicaid rule in Massachusetts, but NHPR reported that case did not seek emergency relief. For the New Hampshire families, the immediate issue is whether coverage can continue through the federal government’s Oct. 13 deadline. The next concrete answers will come from the defendants’ Oct. 15 filing, the Oct. 30 hearing and any subsequent order on the preliminary injunction. Until then, the temporary-restraining-order denial is a procedural ruling, not a final judgment on the policy’s legality or the families’ claims.
location: U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire, Concord
author: NorthEast News Desk
